raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old man, a merchant from the urban area of Cali, Colombia, who had received a hepatic transplant 11 years ago, was admitted to the emergency department because of severe myalgia, paresis of extremities, loss of muscle strength, and progressive deterioration of functional class with gradual limitation of daily activities, permanent fatigue, and mild dyspnea. He also referred since two weeks ago the appearance of jaundice and choluria.
The patient had a history of arterial hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, and obesity. He received hepatic transplantation from a deceased donor 11 years ago after he had a diagnosis with end-stage liver disease due to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Medications included cyclosporine and mycophenolate with poor adherence.
On examination, the patient was disorientated and somnolent. He was transferred to the intensive-care unit. The temperature was 36.3 C, blood pressure 150/100 mmHg, pulse 84 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. White blood cell count was 18990/uL (with 86,5% neutrophils and 5,20% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 16,9 g/dL, platelet count 268000/uL, and C-reactive protein (PCR) 0.64 (normal, 127 0-0.5 mg/dL). The serum level of aspartate aminotransferase was 999 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 511 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 53 U/L, and creatine phosphokinase 10302 U/L. Ultrasonography of the abdomen, eco-Doppler, and cholangioresonance were normal. The contrasted magnetic brain resonance showed nonspecific hyperintensity in the frontal subcortical white matter, and the lumbar puncture was normal. A multifactorial delirium was considered. Statin myopathy and graft rejection were suspected in the beginning; however, the hepatic biopsy was negative for graft rejection. In the search for infectious causes, cultures were taken. The urine and blood cultures were positive for K. pneumoniae and E. coli, both sensitive to ceftriaxone. Two days later, the microbiology laboratory informed that the blood cultures were also positive for Brucella melitensis. After identification of B. melitensis as the causative organism, doxycycline and gentamicin were added to manage, and rifampicin was contraindicated due to the severe hepatic dysfunction. The course was complicated by acute renal failure (creatine 4.15 mg/dL), requiring hemodialysis, and gentamicin was stopped. Ciprofloxacin was added in change. He developed respiratory failure, and he required mechanical ventilation and vasoactive support. The antimicrobial therapy escalated to linezolid, meropenem, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, and caspofungin. New cultures were negative. He developed ascites causing him compression of the inguinal canal and scrotal edema. He was not in a condition for surgery. After a month of hospitalization and in the context of septic shock with multiorgan failure, the patient died.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old male liver transplant recipient presented with severe myalgias, extremity paresis, progressive functional decline, fatigue, mild dyspnea, and two weeks of jaundice and choluria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, a liver transplant recipient from 11 years prior, presented with progressive loss of muscle strength, extremity paresis, severe myalgia, persistent fatigue, mild dyspnea, and gradual limitation of daily activities. Two weeks prior to admission, he noticed the onset of jaundice and dark urine (choluria). Upon presentation, he exhibited disorientation and somnolence requiring intensive care unit admission. During hospitalization, he developed acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis, respiratory failure necessitating mechanical ventilation, septic shock requiring vasopressors, and tense ascites with scrotal edema, resulting in death after one month of hospitalization.
subjective.past_medical_history: Deceased donor orthotopic liver transplantation 11 years prior for end-stage liver disease due to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD); arterial hypertension; type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypothyroidism; hyperlipidemia; obesity. Occupation/Residence: Merchant from urban Cali, Colombia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Jaundice, choluria, permanent fatigue, and mild dyspnea. Home medications: Cyclosporine and mycophenolate mofetil (with poor adherence). Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: Temperature 36.3 °C, blood pressure 150/100 mmHg, pulse 84 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. General: Disoriented and somnolent. Systemic: Jaundice, ascites causing compression of the inguinal canal, and scrotal edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: White blood cell count 18,990/uL (86.5% neutrophils, 5.20% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 16.9 g/dL, platelet count 268,000/uL, C-reactive protein (PCR) 0.64 mg/dL (normal 0-0.5 mg/dL). AST 999 U/L, ALT 511 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 53 U/L, creatine phosphokinase (CPK) 10,302 U/L. Subsequent labs: Serum creatinine rose to 4.15 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasonography and Doppler echo: Normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (cholangioresonance): Normal. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI: Nonspecific hyperintensity in frontal subcortical white matter. Lumbar puncture: CSF examination was normal. Liver graft biopsy: Negative for acute or chronic graft rejection.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellosis with Brucella melitensis bacteremia, alongside co-infections with Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli (both sensitive to ceftriaxone) in urine and blood cultures. Statin myopathy and graft rejection were initially suspected; graft rejection was excluded by negative hepatic biopsy.
Plan & Clinical Course: Ceftriaxone was initiated for K. pneumoniae and E. coli. Following blood culture identification of Brucella melitensis, oral doxycycline and IV gentamicin were added (rifampicin contraindicated due to severe hepatic dysfunction). Course deteriorated with acute renal failure (creatinine 4.15 mg/dL) requiring hemodialysis; gentamicin was stopped and substituted with ciprofloxacin. Patient developed septic shock, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressors, and antimicrobial therapy was escalated to linezolid, meropenem, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, and caspofungin. Repeat cultures became negative. Tense ascites caused inguinal compression and scrotal edema; he was not a surgical candidate. The patient died from multiorgan failure after 1 month of hospitalization.
